blocks.text: [II, 617] Now we shall treat the migration of cranes, with reference to Ierem. VIII, 7. The turtledove, and the swallow, and the crane have kept the time of their coming. In general it is agreed that the crane not only migrates elsewhere, but also travels to the most remote places to escape the cold. Symeon Seth: Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον πτηνὸν διέρχεται τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν, μὴ μένον ἐν ἑνὶ κλίματι [To de toiouton ptēnon dierchetai tēn oikoumenēn hapasan, mē menon en heni klimati]; This bird traverses the whole world, by no means staying in one region. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Ἐκτοπίζουσιν εἰς τὰ ἔσχατα ἐκ τῶν ἐσχάτων [Ektopizousin eis ta eschata ek tōn eschatōn]; They (the cranes) migrate from the farthest regions to the farthest. That is, as he himself explains, ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ [ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei], from the Scythian shores to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. He followed Herodotus, who, treating the sources of the Nile and the neighbouring Ocean in book 2, chapter 22, says: Γέρανοι δὲ φεύγουσαι τὸν χειμῶνα, τὸν ἐν τῇ Σκυθικῇ χώρῃ γενόμενον, φοιτῶσι εἰς χειμαδίην ἐς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Geranoi de pheugousai ton cheimōna, ton en tē Skythikē chōrē genomenon, phoitōsi eis cheimadiēn es tous topous toutous]; Cranes, fleeing the winter of the Scythian region, betake themselves to those places to spend the winter. Aelian too, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 13: Εἰς Αἴγυπτόν τε, καὶ Λιβύην ἀπαίρουσι, καὶ Αἰθιόπιαν, ὥσπερ γὰρ οὖν γῆς περίοδον εἰδυῖαι, καὶ φύσεις ἀέρων, καὶ ὡρῶν διαφορὰς στέλλονται αἱ πᾶσαι [Eis Aigypton te, kai Libyēn apairousi, kai Aithiopian, hōsper gar oun gēs periodon eiduiai, kai physeis aerōn, kai hōrōn diaphoras stellontai hai pasai]; As though they knew the circuit of the earth, the nature of the sky and the variation of the seasons, they depart for Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia, and all set out. And Homer long before:
— — — ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων [tai ge petontai ep᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn],

These fly to the streams of Ocean, namely the southern Ocean, where the Pygmies are, as what follows shows. Hence Lucullus to Pompey in Plutarch: Εἶτά σοι δοκῶ ἐλάττονα τῶν γεράνων νοῦν ἔχειν, καὶ τῶν πελαργῶν, ὥς τε ταῖς ὥραις μὴ συμμεταβάλλειν τὰς διαίτας [Eita soi dokō elattona tōn geranōn noun echein, kai tōn pelargōn, hōs te tais hōrais mē symmetaballein tas diaitas]; Do I seem to you to have less sense than cranes and storks, so as not to change my abode with the seasons of the year?

The ancients believed that most of them are born in Thrace. Aelian, in the place cited above: Αἱ γέρανοι γίνονται μὲν ἐν Θράκῃ [Hai geranoi ginontai men en Thrakē]; Cranes are born in Thrace. And shortly after: Οὐκοῦν φιλοῦσι τὴν χώραν, ἐν ᾗ γεγόνασι [Oukoun philousi tēn chōran, en hē gegonasi]; They therefore love the region in which they were born. Hence they are called birds of Thrace, and Strymonian and Bistonian, from the Strymon, a river, and the Biston, a lake of Thrace, from which they are believed to set out. Virgil, Aeneid, book 10:
— — — as beneath the high clouds Strymonian cranes give their signals. — —
Lucan, book 3, line 199:
The Strymon is deserted, which is wont to commit the Bistonian birds to the warm Nile. — — — [II, 618] And book 5, line 711:
So, when winter drives them out, the cranes leave the icy Strymon, to drink of you, O Nile. — — — —
And book 7, line 832:
— — — you who are wont to exchange Thracian winters for the Nile. — — — —
Martial, cited just now:
Nor the bank that resounds with the Strymonian flock. [col. 71]
Seneca, Oedipus, Act 3:
Not so many birds, fleeing the threats of the icy Strymon, exchange their winters, and, cleaving the sky, offset the Arctic snows with the warm Nile.
Claudian, On the Gildonic War:
— — — — they leave Thrace in summer, when they exchange the Strymon for the warm Nile.
Antipater of Sidon, Anthology, book 3, chapter 16:
— — — — καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστονίαν γέρανον [kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]· — —

And warding off the high-flying Bistonian crane, plunderer of seed. When about to leave Thrace, they are said to gather at the river Hebrus. Aelian, book 2, chapter 1: Ὅταν τὰ ἤθη τὰ τῶν Θρακῶν καὶ τοὺς κρυμοὺς ἀπολείπωσι τοὺς Θρακίους αἱ γέρανοι, ἀθροίζονται μὲν ἐς τὸν Ἕβρον [Hotan ta ēthē ta tōn Thrakōn kai tous krymous apoleipōsi tous Thrakious hai geranoi, athroizontai men es ton Hebron]; When the cranes leave the abodes and the cold of the Thracians, they gather at the Hebrus. Tzetzes, Chiliad 4, Hist. 120:

Ὅταν γοῦν πρὸς τὸν Αἴγυπτον μέλλουσιν ἀποτρέχειν, Ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἕβρον ποταμὸν τὸν Θρακικὸν ἐλθοῦσαι [Hotan goun pros ton Aigypton mellousin apotrechein, Hōs pros ton Hebron potamon ton Thrakikon elthousai]·
When they are about to fly off to Egypt, having come to the Hebrus, a river of Thrace.
But the Scythian cranes take another route, namely across the Pontus, which they fly over. Hence Virgil, Aeneid, book 6:
— — — as when many birds flock to land from the deep sea, when the cold season drives them across the Pontus and sends them to sunny lands.

And it is certain, says Pliny, that when they are about to fly across the Pontus, they first of all make for the narrows between the two promontories Criu-metopon and Carambis. These are only 170,000 paces apart, as he likewise asserts in book 4, chapter 12. [II, 619] Others indeed judge differently, namely that these two promontories are three days' sailing apart, or, what is nearly the same, 2,500 stadia. Dionysius Periegetes, line 155:
Αἵτ' ἄμφω ξυνίασιν ἐναντίαι, οὐ μὲν ἐοῦσαι Ἐγγύθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅσον ὁλκὰς ἐπὶ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἀνύσσῃ [Hait' amphō xyniasin enantiai, ou men eousai Engythen, all᾽ hoson holkas epi triton ēmar anyssē].
